profile.address: Allen, Collin County, Texas (specific street address not independently confirmed this session)
profile.reading:
This is Cisco's data center in Allen, Texas, in Collin County, which opened April 18, 2011. Cisco's own blog and Data Center Knowledge's coverage of the opening do not publish a specific street address for the building, so this registry describes its location only by city, county, and the coordinates already on file rather than asserting an address this research could not independently confirm. The facility was built as an active-active mirror to Cisco's existing Richardson, Texas data center about 15 miles south, with the two sites forming what Cisco calls a Metro Virtual Data Center supporting Cisco IT Elastic Infrastructure Services, the company's internal enterprise and cloud infrastructure, making this an internal corporate data center rather than a public colocation facility.

Cisco's own account of the site describes dual 10 megawatt feeds from two separate electricity providers, arranged as redundant Side A and Side B services rather than as combined additive capacity, while Data Center Knowledge's contemporaneous report on the 2011 opening separately described the building as a 5 megawatt facility. This registry treats those as two different measurements, redundant utility feed capacity on one hand and an actual IT load figure on the other, rather than a factual conflict, and records both honestly instead of picking one. Rooftop solar capacity is also reported inconsistently across the two sources, with Cisco's own blog citing about 400 kilowatts and Data Center Knowledge's opening coverage citing 100 kilowatts, another discrepancy this registry notes rather than resolves. The building uses flywheel based uninterruptible power supply technology providing about 15 seconds of bridging power during an outage, a deliberate contrast with the battery rooms at the sister Richardson facility, and every piece of equipment inside carries separate A and B power feeds with physically separated Side A and Side B network paths.

The facility holds LEED Gold certification, targets a power usage effectiveness of about 1.35, and was engineered to withstand winds up to 175 miles per hour given North Texas tornado risk. It runs on air side economizer cooling that Cisco says avoids mechanical chilling roughly 65 percent of the year, keeps servers at 80 to 82 degrees Fahrenheit, and uses overhead cooling and cable management with no raised floor, plus a rainwater collection lagoon for landscape irrigation. Cisco has said the facility's unified fabric approach, built on its own Unified Computing System and Nexus switching products, saved more than a million dollars in cabling costs compared with a conventional design. No total square footage figure for the building was found in the sourcing reviewed this session. Allen sits in the Dallas Fort Worth metropolitan area, a region that has attracted numerous corporate and technology company data centers over the past two decades due to relatively affordable land and a business friendly Texas tax and regulatory environment.

reading.body:
Cisco Allen is an internal corporate data center opened in 2011 in Allen, Texas, designed as an active-active mirror to Cisco's Richardson facility 15 miles south. The site has dual 10 megawatt utility feeds arranged for redundancy rather than combined capacity, while contemporaneous reporting describes actual IT load as 5 megawatts. At 5 MW of IT load and assuming 10 kW per rack for enterprise infrastructure, the facility holds roughly 500 racks, far below the density required for large-scale AI training workloads.

The campus qualifies under LEED Gold certification, targets a power usage effectiveness of 1.35, and uses air-side economizer cooling to avoid mechanical chilling roughly 65 percent of the year. Every piece of equipment carries separate A and B power feeds with physically isolated network paths, and the building was engineered to withstand 175 mile per hour winds. Cisco has stated the facility's unified fabric design saved over one million dollars in cabling costs compared with conventional architecture, but these specifications describe an internal IT infrastructure site optimized for corporate reliability and efficiency rather than for hosting external AI tenants.

Texas publishes capacity figures for 19 of its 133 mapped facilities, totaling 475 megawatts across the state. Cisco Allen does not appear in the published MW rankings, indicating its 5 megawatt IT load falls below the threshold of facilities Cisco has publicly disclosed specifications for at this site, making it effectively invisible to capacity planners tracking AI infrastructure scaling.
